title: Remember you will die
hook: Stoics, monks and many others kept death in view in order to live better

segments.voice: Yesterday: the overview effect, the whole Earth with no lines on it. Your line was no borders from up there. Did you look up last night? Day one hundred twenty-five.

Walk into an old European painting gallery and you'll start noticing them. A still life: grapes, a lute, a candle, a pocket watch. And, tucked among them, a human skull. Or a portrait of a rich merchant in furs, with a skull on the table beside his hand. The painters weren't being morbid. The skull was a message, and the people who bought the paintings wanted it hanging in their homes, where they'd see it every day. What it said fits in two Latin words. We've spent this week looking at life from above. Today, one of the oldest practices there is. Today: memento mori.
screen: `GRAPES, A LUTE, A CANDLE.` → `AND A SKULL.` → `TWO LATIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Memento mori: remember that you will die. Or, more exactly, remember to die: remember that you are going to. It sounds grim. The people who practiced it said it did the opposite. Let's visit a few of them, each on their own terms. The Stoics made it a daily exercise. Marcus Aurelius reminds himself, more than once, that he could leave life at any moment, and so should let that shape every act and thought. Not in fear: in focus. If this could be the last conversation, you don't waste it on sulking. In Christian monasteries, the Rule of Saint Benedict, written in the sixth century, lists among its tools for good works keeping death daily before one's eyes. For the monks, this was bound up with hope in God and the life to come. The Hebrew Bible has its own version, in Psalm 90. In the King James words: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Counting the days, not to be afraid, but to be wise. In Buddhism, too, monks practice mindfulness of death, maranasati, as a spur to live with care; we'll hear the Buddha's own five remembrances in a few days. These traditions mean very different things by death and what follows it, and we won't blend them. But they share one practical claim. Remembering the end changes the middle. It makes the petty argument look petty. It makes the phone call to your father look urgent. It makes an ordinary Tuesday look like what it is: one of a limited number.
screen: `REMEMBER THAT YOU WILL DIE.` · `THE STOICS: NOT FEAR, FOCUS.` · `BENEDICT: DEATH DAILY BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `NUMBER OUR DAYS.` · then, large: `THE END CHANGES THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, gently. Settle, and breathe. Feel your breath going in and out, a thing that will one day stop. Don't push away any feeling that comes. Then, once, quietly inside: memento mori. Remember you will die. Let it land softly. Then ask: knowing that, what matters today? One person, one task, one kindness. Let the answer come. Then just breathe, alive. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori. Latin for remember you will die, kept in view by Stoics, monks and many others in order to live better. Today's word.
Your line: memento mori. Today, when a small thing starts to eat your hour, say it inside, gently: memento mori. Then spend the hour on what matters. Day one hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Many Stoics, Christian monastics and Buddhist practitioners keep death in view on purpose: through daily reflection, the Rule of Benedict's instruction, the Psalms, or mindfulness of death, each within its own beliefs about what death means.

fork.setup: you're a rich merchant commissioning your portrait. the painter suggests putting a skull on the table beside your hand. what do you say?
options: no: I want to look powerful.
yes: put it where I'll see it every day.
only if it's hidden in the shadows.
fork.reveal: many buyers chose exactly that. the skull wasn't gloom. it was a daily reminder to live well.

original.note: Latin: remember that you will die; more literally, remember to die.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy saying with a skull on it.
what it means: keeping death in view so you spend your limited days on what matters.
what a scholar hears: the Latin phrase itself became common in medieval Christian art; the Stoics taught the idea in Greek and Latin, without the slogan.

sources.quoted: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

sources.ref: Meditations 2.11 (you could depart life this very moment; let that shape every act and thought)
Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 4 (the tools of good works)
maranasati, mindfulness of death (e.g. Anguttara Nikaya 6.19)

notes: Meditations 2.11 and Rule of Benedict ch. 4 ('to keep death daily before one's eyes') are paraphrased; confirm.
AN 6.19 (Maranassati Sutta) cited for mindfulness of death: confirm the reference.

The trapdoor claim that the phrase 'memento mori' is medieval rather than classical: confirm (the Roman triumph story, 'respice post te, hominem te esse memento', is late and uncertain, and is deliberately not told).
Vanitas still lifes and portraits with skulls: mainly 16th–17th century Netherlands; confirm the hook's description.
